gap: No result ChatGPT got works out how often each candidate needs charging once the owner adds a daily 1-hour GPS workout. On that schedule the Fitbit Charge 6's 'up to 7 days' drops to about 3.7 days (about 98 charges a year). The Garmin vívoactive 6 lasts about 7 days (about 51 charges a year). Apple Watch Series 11 and SE 3 still need a daily charge (365 a year), and the SE 3's 18-hour rating can't cover a full day plus a night of sleep tracking.
standout_why: I opened the cited Apple Series 11 tech specs (support.apple.com/125093), the Apple newsroom launch post and the Apple compare page. The cited Google Store Charge 6 spec page and the Charge 6 spec PDF returned no readable text. ChatGPT's answer quotes only the headline maker ratings ('up to 7 days' vs 'up to 24 hours'). Neither the cited Apple specs nor ChatGPT's answer gives battery life under a stated workout routine or charges per year. They also don't show that a GPS smartwatch (vívoactive 6) outlasts the GPS band (Charge 6) once you record a daily workout. I did not open the uncited itechguides, sekin.in, nymag or androidcentral pages, so I can't rule out that one of them has part of this.
decides: It overturns the 'tracker = longer battery' rule for anyone who records a daily GPS workout. In that case the vívoactive 6 smartwatch goes about twice as long between charges as the Charge 6 band (about 7.1 vs 3.7 days). The tracker's battery lead only holds for people who wear it for steps and sleep without daily GPS. Apple Watches need a charge every day either way, and the SE 3's 18-hour rating can't cover a night of sleep tracking without a top-up.

findings.note: Assumes linear drain. 1 ÷ (1/11 + 1/20) = 1 ÷ 0.141 = 7.1 days; 365 ÷ 7.1 = 51 charges. Always-on display: 1 ÷ (1/5 + 1/20) = 4.0 days.
